---
title: "Describing who was excluded"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.align = "center")
has_upset <- requireNamespace("UpSetR", quietly = TRUE)
has_gtsummary <- requireNamespace("gtsummary", quietly = TRUE)
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(cohortflow)

dat <- mock_parallel_rct(n_participants = 300, seed = 2024)
crit <- cf_criteria() |>
  include(~ !is.na(age), label = "Age recorded", category = "Age") |>
  include(~ age >= 18, label = "Aged 18 or over", category = "Age") |>
  include(~ eligible_screen, label = "Passed screening") |>
  include(~ !is.na(consent_date), label = "Consented") |>
  randomise(by = "participant_id", arms = "arm") |>
  exclude(~ withdrew, label = "Withdrew consent") |>
  include(~ baseline_complete, label = "Baseline complete")
flow <- apply_criteria(dat, crit, id = "participant_id")
```

An attrition table says how many people each criterion removed. Readers
and reviewers also ask **who** was removed: did the exclusions change the
make-up of the cohort, and do the reasons overlap? This article covers
three tools for that:

- `as_characteristics_table()`: a "Table 1" with one column per step.
- `criteria_status()`: every row's result on every criterion, for auditing
  and for plotting overlapping reasons.
- `stack_cohorts()`: the cohort at each step, stacked for other
  summary-table packages.

## Table 1 at every step

`as_characteristics_table()` summarises the chosen variables for the cohort
remaining after each step. Numeric variables show the mean (SD), the median
[Q1, Q3], or both; categorical and logical variables show n (%); a
"Missing" row appears when there are missing values.

```{r}
as_characteristics_table(
  flow,
  vars = c("age", "sex", "ethnicity"),
  var_labels = c(age = "Age, years", sex = "Sex", ethnicity = "Ethnicity"),
  numeric = c("mean_sd", "median_iqr"),
  backend = "gt"
)
```

`randomise()` steps are left out by default, since they remove nobody.

### Choosing the columns

`steps` picks and orders the columns, using the same selectors as
`cohort()`: a step number (`0` is the starting data), a step label or a
category name. When you mix numbers and labels, put them in a `list()`, since
`c()` would turn the numbers into text:

```{r}
as_characteristics_table(
  flow,
  vars = c("age", "sex"),
  steps = list(0, "Consented", "Baseline complete"),
  backend = "gt"
)
```

### The people removed at each step

`excluded = TRUE` describes the rows removed *at* each step instead. This is
the usual supplementary table comparing excluded and included participants:

```{r}
as_characteristics_table(
  flow,
  vars = c("age", "sex"),
  excluded = TRUE,
  backend = "gt"
)
```

The people excluded for "Aged 18 or over" have a mean age of about 10, as
they should: a quick check that the criterion did what was intended.

### As data

`as_characteristics_tibble()` returns the same numbers. The long form has
one row per variable, level and step, with separate count, percentage and
display columns, ready for your own formatting or calculation:

```{r}
long <- as_characteristics_tibble(flow, vars = "sex", steps = list(0, "Baseline complete"))
long
```

Use `wide = TRUE` for one column per step, as displayed.

## Every row on every criterion

The cascade records only the *first* criterion each person failed. Someone
under 18 who also never consented is counted only under age, and their
missing consent is never recorded. `criteria_status()` shows the full
picture, with one row per person and one column per criterion.

In the default **cumulative** mode it mirrors the cascade: `TRUE` = reached
the step and passed, `FALSE` = removed there, `NA` = never reached it.

```{r}
criteria_status(flow)
```

In **independent** mode, every criterion is evaluated against everyone,
regardless of the order of the steps. That shows how much the reasons
overlap. The cascade puts 27 removals at "Consented", but 56 people never
consented: the other 29 had already been removed for other reasons.

```{r}
fails <- criteria_status(flow, mode = "independent", sets = "fail",
                         na = "false", as = "matrix")

# How many people fail each criterion
colSums(fails)

# How many criteria each person fails
table(failed = rowSums(fails))
```

The arguments shape the result for whatever comes next:

| Argument | Choices |
|---|---|
| `sets` | `"pass"` (`TRUE` = met the criterion) or `"fail"` (`TRUE` = a reason for exclusion) |
| `na` | `"keep"`, `"false"` (treat not-assessed or `NA` as `FALSE`) or `"drop"` rows with any `NA` |
| `names` | Columns named by step `"label"` or `"step"` number |
| `keep_data` | Also carry the original data columns |
| `as` | `"tibble"`, `"data.table"` or a logical `"matrix"` |

Grouped steps (`group_include()`, `group_exclude()`, `select_within()`)
depend on who else is in the group, so in independent mode they can give a
different answer than in the cascade, where earlier steps had already
removed some group members.

### Plotting overlapping reasons

The matrix plugs straight into set-overlap plots such as
[UpSetR](https://cran.r-project.org/package=UpSetR),
[ComplexUpset](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ComplexUpset) or
[eulerr](https://cran.r-project.org/package=eulerr):

```{r, eval = has_upset, warning = FALSE, fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 4.2, fig.alt = "UpSet plot of exclusion reasons: bars show how many people fail each combination of criteria."}
UpSetR::upset(as.data.frame(fails * 1), nsets = ncol(fails), order.by = "freq")
```

## Other summary-table packages

`stack_cohorts()` returns the cohort at each step stacked into one data
frame with a `step` column, which is the shape that
[gtsummary](https://www.danieldsjoberg.com/gtsummary/) and similar packages
expect:

```{r}
stacked <- stack_cohorts(flow, steps = list(0, "Consented", "Baseline complete"))
table(stacked$step)
```

```{r, eval = has_gtsummary}
gtsummary::tbl_summary(stacked, by = step, include = c(age, sex, ethnicity))
```

A person appears once for every step they survived, so the columns are not
independent samples. Use these tables to describe the cohort, not to test
for differences between columns.
